name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q01 - Electric field inside and outside hollow metal sphere

questiontext.text: A hollow metal sphere of radius \( R \) is uniformly charged. The electric field due to the sphere at a distance \( r \) from the centre

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Inside a uniformly charged hollow metal sphere of radius \( R \), the electrostatic potential is constant throughout the interior volume and equal to its value at the surface. Consequently, the electric field intensity inside the shell (\( r < R \)) is zero everywhere.

Evaluation
Outside the sphere (\( r > R \)), the entire charge behaves as if concentrated at the center. The electric field is given by Coulomb's law: \( E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2} \). Thus, as distance \( r \) increases for \( r > R \), the magnitude of the field decreases inversely proportional to \( r^2 \).

Final Conclusion
The electric field due to the sphere is zero as \( r \) increases for \( r < R \), and decreases as \( r \) increases for \( r > R \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q02 - Work done by a variable force along y direction

questiontext.text: A force \( F = 20 + 10y \) acts on a particle in \( y \)-direction where \( F \) is in newton and \( y \) in meter. Work done by this force to move the particle from \( y = 0 \) to \( y = 1\text{ m} \) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Force expression: \( F = 20 + 10y \text{ N} \)
Initial position: \( y_i = 0\text{ m} \)
Final position: \( y_f = 1\text{ m} \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The force acts along the positive \( y \)-direction, and the displacement occurs along the positive \( y \)-axis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Work done by a position-dependent variable force is defined by: \[ W = \int_{y_i}^{y_f} F \, dy \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the force function into the integral: \[ W = \int_0^1 (20 + 10y) \, dy \] \[ W = \left[ 20y + 5y^2 \right]_0^1 \] \[ W = (20(1) + 5(1)^2) - (0) = 20 + 5 = 25\text{ J} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The total work done by the force to displace the particle from \( y = 0 \) to \( y = 1\text{ m} \) is \( 25\text{ J} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q03 - Power consumption ratio of glowing bulbs

questiontext.text: Six similar bulbs are connected as shown in the figure with a DC source of emf \( E \), and zero internal resistance. The ratio of power consumption by the bulbs when (i) all are glowing and (ii) in the situation when two from section A and one from section B are glowing, will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Let the resistance of each identical bulb be \( R \).
DC source voltage = \( E \), internal resistance = \( 0 \).
Section A has 3 bulbs connected in parallel, and Section B has 3 bulbs connected in parallel. Sections A and B are in series connection across the source.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Power consumed by the combination connected across constant emf \( E \) is given by \( P = \frac{E^2}{R_{\text{eq}}} \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Equivalent resistance of \( n \) identical resistors in parallel: \( R_p = \frac{R}{n} \).
Total equivalent resistance of series sections: \( R_{\text{eq}} = R_A + R_B \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Case (i): All 6 bulbs glowing.
Resistance of section A: \( R_A = \frac{R}{3} \).
Resistance of section B: \( R_B = \frac{R}{3} \).
Total equivalent resistance: \[ R_{\text{eq1}} = \frac{R}{3} + \frac{R}{3} = \frac{2R}{3} \]
Power consumption in Case (i): \[ P_1 = \frac{E^2}{R_{\text{eq1}}} = \frac{E^2}{\frac{2R}{3}} = \frac{3E^2}{2R} \]

Case (ii): Two bulbs from section A and one bulb from section B glowing.
Resistance of section A: \( R_A' = \frac{R}{2} \).
Resistance of section B: \( R_B' = R \).
Total equivalent resistance: \[ R_{\text{eq2}} = \frac{R}{2} + R = \frac{3R}{2} \]
Power consumption in Case (ii): \[ P_2 = \frac{E^2}{R_{\text{eq2}}} = \frac{E^2}{\frac{3R}{2}} = \frac{2E^2}{3R} \]

Ratio of power consumption \( P_1 : P_2 \): \[ \frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{\frac{3E^2}{2R}}{\frac{2E^2}{3R}} = \frac{3}{2} \times \frac{3}{2} = \frac{9}{4} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The ratio of power consumption between the two situations is \( 9:4 \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q04 - Depth of water corresponding to excess pressure in soap bubble

questiontext.text: A soap bubble, having radius of \( 1\text{ mm} \), is blown from a detergent solution having a surface tension of \( 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\text{ N/m} \). The pressure inside the bubble equals at a point \( Z_0 \) below the free surface of water in a container. Taking \( g = 10\text{ m/s}^2 \), density of water \( = 10^3\text{ kg/m}^3 \), the value of \( Z_0 \) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of soap bubble \( r = 1\text{ mm} = 10^{-3}\text{ m} \)
Surface tension \( T = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\text{ N/m} \)
Acceleration due to gravity \( g = 10\text{ m/s}^2 \)
Density of water \( \rho = 10^3\text{ kg/m}^3 \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Atmospheric pressure is \( P_0 \). A soap bubble has two spherical interfaces (inner and outer liquid surfaces).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Excess pressure inside a soap bubble: \[ \Delta P = \frac{4T}{r} \]
Total pressure inside the bubble: \[ P_{\text{in}} = P_0 + \frac{4T}{r} \]
Hydrostatic pressure at depth \( Z_0 \) in water: \[ P_{\text{water}} = P_0 + \rho g Z_0 \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Equate the pressure inside the bubble to the pressure at depth \( Z_0 \): \[ P_0 + \frac{4T}{r} = P_0 + \rho g Z_0 \implies \rho g Z_0 = \frac{4T}{r} \]
Substitute given numerical values: \[ \frac{4T}{r} = \frac{4 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\text{ N/m}}{10^{-3}\text{ m}} = 100\text{ N/m}^2 \]
Equating hydrostatic pressure difference: \[ (10^3\text{ kg/m}^3) \times (10\text{ m/s}^2) \times Z_0 = 100\text{ N/m}^2 \] \[ 10^4 Z_0 = 100 \implies Z_0 = \frac{100}{10^4} = 10^{-2}\text{ m} = 1\text{ cm} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The depth \( Z_0 \) below the free surface of water is \( 1\text{ cm} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q05 - Wavelength order of visible light spectrum

questiontext.text: Which colour of the light has the longest wavelength?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
In the visible spectrum of electromagnetic radiation, wavelength increases continuously from violet to red light according to the relation \( c = \nu \lambda \).

Evaluation
The approximate range of wavelengths for visible spectrum colors is:
- Violet: \( 380 - 450\text{ nm} \)
- Blue: \( 450 - 495\text{ nm} \)
- Green: \( 495 - 570\text{ nm} \)
- Red: \( 620 - 750\text{ nm} \)
Red light possesses the lowest frequency and therefore the longest wavelength among all visible spectrum colors.

Final Conclusion
Red light has the longest wavelength.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q06 - Acceleration due to gravity and weight at depth

questiontext.text: A body weight 200 N on the surface of earth. How much will it weight half way down to the centre of the earth?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Weight of body on Earth's surface \( W = mg = 200\text{ N} \).
Depth below surface \( d = \frac{R}{2} \), where \( R \) is the radius of the Earth.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Earth is assumed to be a uniform sphere of uniform mass density.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Acceleration due to gravity at depth \( d \) inside the Earth is given by: \[ g' = g \left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right) \]
The weight at depth \( d \) is: \[ W' = mg' \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \( d = \frac{R}{2} \) into the gravity formula: \[ g' = g \left(1 - \frac{R/2}{R}\right) = g \left(1 - \frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{g}{2} \]
Calculate the weight at depth \( d \): \[ W' = m\left(\frac{g}{2}\right) = \frac{mg}{2} = \frac{200\text{ N}}{2} = 100\text{ N} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Halfway down to the center of the Earth, the acceleration due to gravity halves, so the weight of the body becomes \( 100\text{ N} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q07 - Rate of flow of water from orifice near bottom

questiontext.text: A small hole of area of cross-section 2 mm² present near the bottom of a fully filled open tank of height 2 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², the rate of flow of water through the open hole would be nearly

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Area of cross-section of hole \( A = 2\text{ mm}^2 = 2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2 \)
Height of water column \( h = 2\text{ m} \)
Acceleration due to gravity \( g = 10\text{ m/s}^2 \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Water is treated as an ideal incompressible, non-viscous fluid flowing under Torricelli's theorem conditions.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Speed of efflux from a small hole at depth \( h \): \[ v = \sqrt{2gh} \]
Volume flow rate (rate of flow): \[ Q = A \cdot v \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate speed of efflux: \[ v = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 2} = \sqrt{40} \approx 6.3245\text{ m/s} \]
Calculate volume flow rate: \[ Q = (2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2) \times (6.3245\text{ m/s}) \approx 12.649 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3\text{/s} \approx 12.6 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3\text{/s} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The rate of flow of water through the hole is approximately \( 12.6 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3\text{/s} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q08 - Work required to stop a rolling disc

questiontext.text: A disc of radius 2 m and mass 100 kg rolls on a horizontal floor. Its centre of mass has speed of 20 cm/s. How much work is needed to stop it?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of disc \( m = 100\text{ kg} \)
Radius of disc \( R = 2\text{ m} \)
Speed of centre of mass \( v = 20\text{ cm/s} = 0.2\text{ m/s} \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The disc undergoes pure rolling without slipping on a horizontal plane surface.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total kinetic energy of a rolling body: \[ K_{\text{total}} = K_{\text{trans}} + K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 \]
For a solid disc, moment of inertia \( I = \frac{1}{2} m R^2 \), and pure rolling condition yields \( \omega = \frac{v}{R} \).
By the Work-Energy theorem, work required to bring the body to rest equals its total initial kinetic energy: \( W = K_{\text{total}} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \( I \) and \( \omega \) into kinetic energy: \[ K_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{1}{2} m R^2\right)\left(\frac{v}{R}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{4} m v^2 = \frac{3}{4} m v^2 \]
Substitute numerical values: \[ W = \frac{3}{4} \times 100 \times (0.2)^2 = 75 \times 0.04 = 3\text{ J} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The work required to stop the rolling disc is \( 3\text{ J} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q09 - Equivalent focal length of thin lens combination with liquid

questiontext.text: Two similar thin equi-convex lenses, of focal length \( f \) each, are kept coaxially in contact with each other such that the focal length of the combination is \( F_1 \). When the space between the two lenses is filled with glycerin (which has the same refractive index (\( \mu = 1.5 \)) as that of glass) then the equivalent focal length is \( F_2 \). The ratio \( F_1 : F_2 \) will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Focal length of each equi-convex glass lens = \( f \)
Refractive index of glass \( \mu_g = 1.5 \)
Refractive index of glycerin \( \mu_l = 1.5 \)
Combination 1: Two convex lenses in contact without glycerin, equivalent focal length = \( F_1 \).
Combination 2: Space between lenses filled with glycerin, equivalent focal length = \( F_2 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Lenses are thin and kept coaxially in contact. Cartesian sign convention applies.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Lens Maker's Formula: \[ \frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right) \]
Equivalent focal length of thin lenses in contact: \[ \frac{1}{F} = \sum \frac{1}{f_i} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For Combination 1 (two convex glass lenses): \[ \frac{1}{F_1} = \frac{1}{f} + \frac{1}{f} = \frac{2}{f} \implies F_1 = \frac{f}{2} \]
2. Find radius of curvature \( R \) of equi-convex glass lens: \[ \frac{1}{f} = (1.5 - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R} - \left(-\frac{1}{R}\right)\right) = 0.5 \times \frac{2}{R} = \frac{1}{R} \implies R = f \]
3. The glycerin filled in the gap forms an equi-concave liquid lens with radii of curvature \( -R \) and \( +R \). Its focal length \( f_l \) is: \[ \frac{1}{f_l} = (1.5 - 1)\left(-\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{R}\right) = 0.5 \times \left(-\frac{2}{R}\right) = -\frac{1}{R} = -\frac{1}{f} \implies f_l = -f \]
4. For Combination 2 (two convex glass lenses + one concave liquid lens in contact): \[ \frac{1}{F_2} = \frac{1}{f} + \frac{1}{f_l} + \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{f} + \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f} \implies F_2 = f \]
5. Ratio \( F_1 : F_2 \): \[ \frac{F_1}{F_2} = \frac{f/2}{f} = \frac{1}{2} = 1:2 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The ratio \( F_1 : F_2 \) is \( 1:2 \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q10 - Maximum percentage error calculation in composite physical quantity

questiontext.text: In an experiment, the percentage of error occurred in the measurement of physical quantities A, B, C and D are 1%, 2%, 3% and 4% respectively. Then the maximum percentage of error in the measurement X, where \( X = \frac{A^2 B^{1/2}}{C^{1/3} D^3} \), will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Physical quantity relation: \[ X = \frac{A^2 B^{1/2}}{C^{1/3} D^3} \]
Percentage errors:
\( \frac{\Delta A}{A} \times 100 = 1\% \)
\( \frac{\Delta B}{B} \times 100 = 2\% \)
\( \frac{\Delta C}{C} \times 100 = 3\% \)
\( \frac{\Delta D}{D} \times 100 = 4\% \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Maximum percentage error is calculated by adding the absolute maximum fractional errors of each independent variable weighted by their respective power exponents.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a expression \( X = A^a B^b C^{-c} D^{-d} \), maximum percentage error is: \[ \frac{\Delta X}{X} \times 100 = |a| \left(\frac{\Delta A}{A}\times 100\right) + |b| \left(\frac{\Delta B}{B}\times 100\right) + |c| \left(\frac{\Delta C}{C}\times 100\right) + |d| \left(\frac{\Delta D}{D}\times 100\right) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute exponents and values into the equation: \[ \frac{\Delta X}{X} \times 100 = 2(1\%) + \frac{1}{2}(2\%) + \frac{1}{3}(3\%) + 3(4\%) \] \[ \frac{\Delta X}{X} \times 100 = 2\% + 1\% + 1\% + 12\% = 16\% \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The maximum percentage error in \( X \) is \( 16\% \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q11 - SI unit of thermal conductivity

questiontext.text: The unit of thermal conductivity is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Physical quantity: Thermal Conductivity (\( K \)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Heat flows in steady state across a material of cross-sectional area \( A \) and thickness \( L \) under a temperature difference \( \Delta T \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Heat transfer rate equation: \[ \frac{Q}{t} = K \frac{A \Delta T}{L} \implies K = \frac{Q}{t} \cdot \frac{L}{A \Delta T} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Identify SI units of constituent variables:
- Rate of heat flow \( \frac{Q}{t} \): Watt (\text{W})
- Thickness \( L \): meter (\text{m})
- Area \( A \): square meter (\text{m}^2)
- Temperature difference \( \Delta T \): Kelvin (\text{K})

Substitute SI units into the formula for \( K \): \[ [K] = \frac{\text{W} \cdot \text{m}}{\text{m}^2 \cdot \text{K}} = \text{W m}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The SI unit of thermal conductivity is \( \text{W m}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q12 - Work done to raise mass to height equal to radius of Earth

questiontext.text: The work done to raise a mass \( m \) from the surface of the earth to a height \( h \), which is equal to the radius of the earth, is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of body = \( m \)
Height above Earth's surface \( h = R \), where \( R \) is the radius of Earth.
Acceleration due to gravity at surface = \( g \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Gravitational potential energy is zero at infinite separation. The gravitational field varies with distance for height comparable to Earth's radius.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Gravitational potential energy at distance \( r \) from Earth's center: \[ U(r) = -\frac{GMm}{r} \]
Work done by external force equals change in potential energy: \[ W = \Delta U = U_f - U_i \]
Relation between gravitational constant and surface gravity: \( GM = gR^2 \)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Initial position (surface): \( r_i = R \implies U_i = -\frac{GMm}{R} \)
Final position (height \( h = R \)): \( r_f = R + R = 2R \implies U_f = -\frac{GMm}{2R} \)
Calculate work done: \[ W = -\frac{GMm}{2R} - \left(-\frac{GMm}{R}\right) = \frac{GMm}{2R} \]
Substitute \( GM = gR^2 \): \[ W = \frac{(gR^2) m}{2R} = \frac{1}{2} mgR \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The work done to raise the mass to height equal to the radius of Earth is \( \frac{1}{2} mgR \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q13 - Thermodynamic process with no heat exchange

questiontext.text: In which of the following processes, heat is neither absorbed nor released by a system?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
By definition in thermodynamics, an adiabatic process is one in which no heat energy crosses the boundary of the system (\( \Delta Q = 0 \)).

Evaluation
- Isobaric process: pressure remains constant; heat is exchanged with surroundings (\( Q = n C_p \Delta T \)).
- Isochoric process: volume remains constant; heat is exchanged with surroundings (\( Q = n C_v \Delta T \)).
- Isothermal process: temperature remains constant; heat exchange equals work done (\( Q = W \)).
- Adiabatic process: system is thermally insulated from surroundings, so heat is neither absorbed nor released.

Final Conclusion
An adiabatic process is the thermodynamic process where heat is neither absorbed nor released.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q14 - Force between point charges after charge transfer

questiontext.text: Two point charges A and B, having charges \( +Q \) and \( -Q \) respectively, are placed at certain distance apart and force acting between them is F. If \( 25\% \) charge of A is transferred to B, then force between the charges becomes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial charge of A: \( Q_A = +Q \)
Initial charge of B: \( Q_B = -Q \)
Initial distance: \( r \)
Initial electrostatic force magnitude: \( F \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Coulomb's Law applies to stationary point charges in free space.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Coulomb's Law: \[ F = k \frac{|Q_A Q_B|}{r^2} = k \frac{Q^2}{r^2} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Amount of charge transferred from A to B: \( \Delta Q = 0.25 Q = \frac{Q}{4} \)
New charge on A: \[ Q_A' = Q - \frac{Q}{4} = \frac{3}{4} Q \]
New charge on B: \[ Q_B' = -Q + \frac{Q}{4} = -\frac{3}{4} Q \]
Calculate new electrostatic force magnitude \( F' \): \[ F' = k \frac{|Q_A' Q_B'|}{r^2} = k \frac{\left(\frac{3}{4} Q\right)\left(\frac{3}{4} Q\right)}{r^2} = \frac{9}{16} \left(k \frac{Q^2}{r^2}\right) = \frac{9F}{16} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The force between the charges becomes \( \frac{9F}{16} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q15 - Boolean logic operation of LED circuit

questiontext.text: The correct Boolean operation represented by the circuit diagram drawn is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A DC voltage source of \( +6\text{ V} \) is connected to two resistors \( R \) and an LED (\( Y \)).
Two switches \( A \) and \( B \) can take state 0 (open) or state 1 (connected to common line).

Step 2: Circuit Analysis and Truth Table Construction
- When \( A = 0 \) and \( B = 0 \): Both switches are open. Current flows from \( +6\text{ V} \) through the upper resistor, LED, and lower resistor to ground. The LED glows, giving output \( Y = 1 \).
- When \( A = 1 \) and \( B = 0 \): Upper node is connected to the common line, but lower node remains ungrounded via switch B. Current continues to flow through the LED, so \( Y = 1 \).
- When \( A = 0 \) and \( B = 1 \): Lower node is connected to the common line, but upper node is not connected to common line via switch A. Current continues to flow through the LED, so \( Y = 1 \).
- When \( A = 1 \) and \( B = 1 \): Both switches connect both terminals of the LED directly to the same common line, effectively short-circuiting the LED. Potential difference across the LED becomes zero, so no current passes through it and the LED turns off, giving output \( Y = 0 \).

Step 3: Boolean Evaluation
The output is 0 only when both inputs are 1, and 1 for all other input combinations. This matches the truth table of a NAND operation: \[ Y = \overline{A \cdot B} \]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The logic circuit represents a NAND gate.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q16 - Identification of circuit protection device

questiontext.text: Which of the following acts as a circuit protection device?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
A circuit protection device protects electrical circuits and components by automatically breaking the current flow whenever an overcurrent or short-circuit condition occurs.

Evaluation
- Inductor: stores energy in a magnetic field and opposes changes in current, but does not disconnect the circuit.
- Switch: manually opens or closes a circuit under normal operation.
- Fuse: contains a metallic strip with a low melting point that melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds a safe value.
- Conductor: carries electric current without intention of breaking.

Final Conclusion
A fuse acts as a circuit protection device.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q17 - Thermal expansion and temperature independent length difference

questiontext.text: A copper rod of \( 88\text{ cm} \) and an aluminium rod of unknown length have their increase in length independent of increase in temperature. The length of aluminium rod is (\( \alpha_{\text{Cu}} = 1.7 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1} \) and \( \alpha_{\text{Al}} = 2.2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1} \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length of copper rod \( L_{\text{Cu}} = 88\text{ cm} \)
Coefficient of linear expansion of copper \( \alpha_{\text{Cu}} = 1.7 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1} \)
Coefficient of linear expansion of aluminium \( \alpha_{\text{Al}} = 2.2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1} \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The condition that the difference in lengths remains constant for any temperature change \( \Delta T \) requires the absolute expansion in both rods to be equal: \( \Delta L_{\text{Cu}} = \Delta L_{\text{Al}} \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Linear expansion formula: \[ \Delta L = L \alpha \Delta T \]
Equating expansions: \[ L_{\text{Cu}} \alpha_{\text{Cu}} \Delta T = L_{\text{Al}} \alpha_{\text{Al}} \Delta T \implies L_{\text{Cu}} \alpha_{\text{Cu}} = L_{\text{Al}} \alpha_{\text{Al}} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Rearrange for \( L_{\text{Al}} \): \[ L_{\text{Al}} = \frac{L_{\text{Cu}} \alpha_{\text{Cu}}}{\alpha_{\text{Al}}} \]
Substitute numerical values: \[ L_{\text{Al}} = \frac{88\text{ cm} \times (1.7 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1})}{2.2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}} = \frac{88}{2.2} \times 1.7 = 40 \times 1.7 = 68\text{ cm} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The length of the aluminium rod is \( 68\text{ cm} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q18 - Conduction and displacement current in charging capacitor

questiontext.text: A parallel plate capacitor of capacitance \( 20\ \mu\text{F} \) is being charged by a voltage source whose potential is changing at the rate of \( 3\text{ V/s} \). The conduction current through the connecting wires, and the displacement current through the plates of the capacitor, would be, respectively

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Capacitance \( C = 20\ \mu\text{F} = 20 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F} \)
Rate of potential change \( \frac{dV}{dt} = 3\text{ V/s} \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Conduction current \( I_c \) flows in the connecting wires while displacement current \( I_d \) exists in the dielectric region between capacitor plates.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Conduction current: \[ I_c = \frac{dq}{dt} = C \frac{dV}{dt} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate conduction current \( I_c \): \[ I_c = (20 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}) \times (3\text{ V/s}) = 60 \times 10^{-6}\text{ A} = 60\ \mu\text{A} \]
Since displacement current equals conduction current: \[ I_d = 60\ \mu\text{A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The conduction current and displacement current are respectively \( 60\ \mu\text{A} \) and \( 60\ \mu\text{A} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q20 - Minimum angular velocity of rotating cylinder to hold block

questiontext.text: A block of mass 10 kg is in contact against the inner wall of a hollow cylindrical drum of radius 1 m. The coefficient of friction between the block and the inner wall of the cylinder is 0.1. The minimum angular velocity needed for the cylinder to keep the block stationary when the cylinder is vertical and rotating about its axis, will be (\( g = 10\text{ m/s}^2 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of block \( m = 10\text{ kg} \)
Radius of cylinder \( R = 1\text{ m} \)
Coefficient of static friction \( \mu = 0.1 \)
Acceleration due to gravity \( g = 10\text{ m/s}^2 \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The drum rotates about its vertical axis. The normal force \( N \) exerted by the wall on the block provides the necessary centripetal force. Static friction \( f_s \) acts vertically upward balancing the downward gravitational weight.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Centripetal force: \[ N = m \omega^2 R \]
Vertical equilibrium condition: \[ f_s = mg \]
Maximum static friction limit: \[ f_s \le \mu N \implies mg \le \mu (m \omega^2 R) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Solve for minimum angular velocity \( \omega_{\text{min}} \): \[ mg = \mu m \omega_{\text{min}}^2 R \implies \omega_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{\frac{g}{\mu R}} \]
Substitute numerical values: \[ \omega_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{\frac{10}{0.1 \times 1}} = \sqrt{100} = 10\text{ rad/s} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The minimum angular velocity needed to keep the block stationary is \( 10\text{ rad/s} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q21 - Effect of temperature increase on gas molecules

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q22 - Induced emf in rotating coil in magnetic field

questiontext.text: A 800 turn coil of effective area \( 0.05\text{ m}^2 \) is kept perpendicular to a magnetic field \( 5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T} \). When the plane of the coil is rotated by \( 90^\circ \) around any of its coplanar axis in \( 0.1\text{ s} \), the emf induced in the coil will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Number of turns \( N = 800 \)
Effective area \( A = 0.05\text{ m}^2 \)
Magnetic field \( B = 5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T} \)
Rotation angle \( \Delta \theta = 90^\circ \)
Time interval \( \Delta t = 0.1\text{ s} \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Initially, the normal to the plane of the coil is aligned with the magnetic field (\( \theta_1 = 0^\circ \)). After rotating by \( 90^\circ \), the normal is perpendicular to the field (\( \theta_2 = 90^\circ \)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Initial flux linkage: \[ \Phi_1 = N B A \cos(0^\circ) = N B A \]
Final flux linkage: \[ \Phi_2 = N B A \cos(90^\circ) = 0 \]
Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction (magnitude of induced emf): \[ e = \left| \frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} \right| = \frac{\Phi_1 - \Phi_2}{\Delta t} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate initial flux: \[ \Phi_1 = 800 \times (5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}) \times (0.05\text{ m}^2) = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ Wb} \]
Calculate induced emf magnitude: \[ e = \frac{2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ Wb}}{0.1\text{ s}} = 2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ V} = 0.02\text{ V} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The induced emf in the coil is \( 0.02\text{ V} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q23 - Electric field midway between parallel infinite line charges

questiontext.text: Two parallel infinite line charges with linear charge densities \( +\lambda\text{ C/m} \) and \( -\lambda\text{ C/m} \) are placed at a distance of 2R in free space. What is the electric field mid-way between the two line charges?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Linear charge density of positive line charge = \( +\lambda \)
Linear charge density of negative line charge = \( -\lambda \)
Separation between lines = \( 2R \)
Distance of midpoint from each line = \( R \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The lines are infinitely long and parallel in vacuum. Electric field points away from positive charge and towards negative charge.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Electric field due to an infinite line charge at distance \( R \): \[ E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 R} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Electric field due to positive line charge at midpoint: \[ E_1 = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 R} \quad \text{(directed towards the negative line)} \]
Electric field due to negative line charge at midpoint: \[ E_2 = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 R} \quad \text{(directed towards the negative line)} \]
Since both electric fields point in the same direction, the total electric field magnitude is: \[ E_{\text{total}} = E_1 + E_2 = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 R} + \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 R} = \frac{2\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 R} = \frac{\lambda}{\pi\varepsilon_0 R} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The electric field midway between the two line charges is \( \frac{\lambda}{\pi\varepsilon_0 R}\text{ N/C} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q24 - Angle of refraction at critical angle of incidence

Evaluation
The critical angle \( i_c \) is defined specifically as the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium reaches \( 90^\circ \), causing the refracted light ray to graze along the boundary interface.

Final Conclusion
When the angle of incidence equals the critical angle, the angle of refraction is \( 90^\circ \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q25 - de Broglie wavelength of accelerated electron

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
de-Broglie wavelength of an electron: \[ \lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m_e e V}} = \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{Å} = \frac{12.27 \times 10^{-10}}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ m} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working

The de-Broglie wavelength of the accelerated electron is nearly \( 12.2 \times 10^{-12}\text{ m} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q26 - Variation of magnetic field with distance for solid cylindrical conductor

questiontext.text: A cylindrical conductor of radius R is carrying a constant current. The plot of the magnitude of the magnetic field B with the distance \( d \) from the centre of the conductor, is correctly represented by the figure

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Solid long cylindrical conductor of radius \( R \), carrying a constant uniform current \( I \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Current density \( J = \frac{I}{\pi R^2} \) is uniform across the cross-section of the cylinder.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Ampere's Circuital Law: \[ \oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Inside the conductor (\( d \le R \)):
Current enclosed by Amperian loop of radius \( d \): \[ I_{\text{enclosed}} = I \left(\frac{\pi d^2}{\pi R^2}\right) = I \frac{d^2}{R^2} \]
Applying Ampere's Law: \[ B(2\pi d) = \mu_0 I \frac{d^2}{R^2} \implies B_{\text{in}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R^2} d \]
Thus, \( B_{\text{in}} \propto d \) (magnetic field increases linearly from zero at the axis to maximum at the surface \( d = R \)).

2. Outside the conductor (\( d \ge R \)):
Total current enclosed: \[ I_{\text{enclosed}} = I \]
Applying Ampere's Law: \[ B(2\pi d) = \mu_0 I \implies B_{\text{out}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d} \]
Thus, \( B_{\text{out}} \propto \frac{1}{d} \) (magnetic field decreases inversely with distance outside the cylinder).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct plot shows a linear rise of \( B \) from the origin up to distance \( R \), followed by a hyperbolic decay (\( 1/d \)) for distance greater than \( R \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q29 - Amplitude of simple harmonic oscillation

questiontext.text: The displacement of a particle executing simple harmonic motion is given by \[ y = A_0 + A \sin \omega t + B \cos \omega t. \] Then the amplitude of its oscillation is given by

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Displacement equation: \( y = A_0 + A \sin \omega t + B \cos \omega t \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\( A_0 \) is a constant representing a shift in the mean (equilibrium) position.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Superposition of two perpendicular/orthogonal harmonic components of the same frequency: \[ A \sin \omega t + B \cos \omega t = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2} \sin(\omega t + \phi) \]
where \( \tan \phi = \frac{B}{A} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working

The amplitude is the maximum displacement relative to the mean position \( y - A_0 \): \[ \text{Amplitude} = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The amplitude of oscillation is \( \sqrt{A^2 + B^2} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q31 - Application of eddy currents in electrical devices

questiontext.text: In which of the following devices, the eddy current effect is not used?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
Eddy currents are loops of electrical current induced within bulk conductors by a changing magnetic field. They are intentionally utilized in applications relying on electromagnetic damping or induction heating.

Evaluation
- Magnetic braking in trains uses induced eddy currents to generate opposing magnetic drag.
- Induction furnaces use high-frequency eddy currents to generate intense heat for melting metals.

The eddy current effect is not used in an electric heater.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q32 - Swimmer direction for shortest path across river

If he is standing on the south bank and wishes to cross the river along the shortest path, the angle at which he should make his strokes w.r.t. north is given by

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Swimmer speed relative to still water \( v_s = 20\text{ m/s} \)
River flow velocity \( v_r = 10\text{ m/s} \) due East.
Swimmer starts from South bank wanting to reach North bank along the shortest path (straight across, due North).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let East be along positive \( x \)-axis and North along positive \( y \)-axis. The swimmer heads at an angle \( \theta \) West of North.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For the net velocity vector to point strictly North, the eastward component of swimmer's velocity must exactly cancel the river flow: \[ v_s \sin \theta = v_r \]

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q34 - Voltmeter and ammeter readings in parallel resistance circuits

Circuit 2: A 10 V DC battery connected across a parallel combination: top branch has a \( 10\ \Omega \) resistor, bottom branch has a \( 10\ \Omega \) resistor in series with voltmeter \( V_2 \), and ammeter \( A_2 \) carries main line current \( i_2 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q35 - Fraction of energy lost by colliding body in elastic collision

questiontext.text: Body A of mass 4m moving with speed u collides with another body B of mass 2m, at rest. The collision is head on and elastic in nature. After the collision the fraction of energy lost by the colliding body A is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of body A: \( m_1 = 4m \)
Initial speed of body A: \( u_1 = u \)
Mass of body B: \( m_2 = 2m \)
Initial speed of body B: \( u_2 = 0 \)
Collision type: head-on elastic collision

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Kinetic energy and linear momentum are conserved.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Final velocity of body A after elastic head-on collision: \[ v_1 = \left(\frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_1 + \left(\frac{2m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_2 \]
Fractional energy lost by body A: \[ \frac{\Delta K_A}{K_{A,i}} = \frac{K_{A,i} - K_{A,f}}{K_{A,i}} = 1 - \frac{v_1^2}{u_1^2} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate final velocity \( v_1 \): \[ v_1 = \left(\frac{4m - 2m}{4m + 2m}\right) u = \frac{2m}{6m} u = \frac{u}{3} \]
Calculate final kinetic energy of body A: \[ K_{A,f} = \frac{1}{2} (4m) \left(\frac{u}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{9} \left[\frac{1}{2} (4m) u^2\right] = \frac{1}{9} K_{A,i} \]
Calculate fraction of kinetic energy lost by body A: \[ \frac{\Delta K_A}{K_{A,i}} = 1 - \frac{1}{9} = \frac{8}{9} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The fraction of energy lost by colliding body A is \( \frac{8}{9} \).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because the net force acting on the particle is zero, the velocity of the particle will remain constant.

questiontext.text: A solid cylinder of mass 2 kg and radius 4 cm is rotating about its axis at the rate of 3 rpm. The torque required to stop after \( 2\pi \) revolutions is

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2019_Q44 - Distance traveled up inclined plane for different angles

A disproportionation reaction is a redox reaction in which an element in a single oxidation state is simultaneously oxidized and reduced into two different oxidation states.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2019_Q57 - Increasing order of first ionisation enthalpy for second period

questiontext.text: Which of the following diatomic molecular species has only \( \pi \) bonds according to Molecular Orbital Theory?

Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Diatomic species: \( \text{N}_2 \), \( \text{C}_2 \), \( \text{Be}_2 \), \( \text{O}_2 \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Apply standard Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT) orbital energy filling diagrams.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For diatomic molecules with 14 or fewer electrons, the MO filling sequence is: \[ \sigma 1s < \sigma^* 1s < \sigma 2s < \sigma^* 2s < (\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y) < \sigma 2p_z \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \( \text{C}_2 \) (12 electrons):
- Inner core electrons: \( \sigma 1s^2 \, \sigma^* 1s^2 \, \sigma 2s^2 \, \sigma^* 2s^2 \) (4 bonding, 4 antibonding electrons, net bonding contribution cancels out).
- Valence 4 electrons occupy the degenerate pi subshells: \( (\pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2) \).
Thus, all 4 valence bonding electrons in \( \text{C}_2 \) reside in \( \pi \) molecular orbitals. The double bond in \( \text{C}_2 \) consists exclusively of two \( \pi \) bonds with no \( \sigma \) bond component.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
According to Molecular Orbital Theory, \( \text{C}_2 \) contains only \( \pi \) bonds.

Total pi (\( \pi \)) bonds: \[ 1 (\text{from C=C}) + 2 (\text{from C}\equiv\text{C}) = 3\ \pi\text{ bonds} \]

Pent-2-en-4-yne contains 10 \( \sigma \) bonds and 3 \( \pi \) bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2019_Q62 - Work done during isothermal expansion against constant pressure

questiontext.text: Under isothermal condition, a gas at 300 K expands from 0.1 L to 0.25 L against a constant external pressure of 2 bar. The work done by the gas is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial volume \( V_1 = 0.1\text{ L} = 0.1 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3 \)
Final volume \( V_2 = 0.25\text{ L} = 0.25 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3 \)
External pressure \( P_{\text{ext}} = 2\text{ bar} = 2 \times 10^5\text{ Pa} \)
Temperature \( T = 300\text{ K} \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
IUPAC convention defines work done on the system as \( W = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Irreversible pressure-volume work: \[ W = -P_{\text{ext}} (V_2 - V_1) \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate volume change: \[ \Delta V = 0.25\text{ L} - 0.1\text{ L} = 0.15\text{ L} = 0.15 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3 \]
Calculate work done: \[ W = -(2 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}) \times (0.15 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3) = -300\text{ J} \quad \text{or } -30\text{ J} \]
Using bar-litre conversion (\( 1\text{ bar L} = 100\text{ J} \)): \[ W = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V = -(2\text{ bar}) \times (0.15\text{ L}) = -0.30\text{ bar L} = -0.30 \times 100\text{ J} = -30\text{ J} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The work done by the gas is \( -30\text{ J} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_2019_Q69 - Time required for 99 percent completion of first order reaction

Percentage completion = \( 99\% \)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The reaction follows first-order chemical kinetics.

Integrated rate law for a first-order reaction: \[ t = \frac{2.303}{k} \log_{10} \left(\frac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}\right) \]

The time required for 99% completion is \( t = \frac{4.606}{k} \).

The reaction \( 2\text{H}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{H}_2(\text{g}) \) has a negative entropy change.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_2019_Q94 - Genotypic frequencies calculation using Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium

questiontext.text: A gene locus has two alleles A, a. If the frequency of dominant allele A is 0.4, then what will be the frequency of homozygous dominant, heterozygous and homozygous recessive individuals in the population?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Dominant allele frequency, \(p = f(A) = 0.4\).
Gene locus contains two alleles: dominant \(A\) and recessive \(a\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Assume the population adheres to Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
The total allelic frequency satisfies \(p + q = 1\), where \(q = f(a)\).
Genotypic frequencies satisfy \(p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Frequency of recessive allele: \(q = 1 - p\)
Frequency of homozygous dominant genotype: \(f(AA) = p^2\)
Frequency of heterozygous genotype: \(f(Aa) = 2pq\)
Frequency of homozygous recessive genotype: \(f(aa) = q^2\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate \(q\):
\[ q = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6 \]
2. Calculate frequency of homozygous dominant \(AA\):
\[ f(AA) = (0.4)^2 = 0.16 \]
3. Calculate frequency of heterozygous \(Aa\):
\[ f(Aa) = 2 \times 0.4 \times 0.6 = 0.48 \]
4. Calculate frequency of homozygous recessive \(aa\):
\[ f(aa) = (0.6)^2 = 0.36 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Sum of genotypic frequencies: \(0.16 + 0.48 + 0.36 = 1.00\).
The respective genotypic frequencies in the population are \(0.16\) for \(AA\), \(0.48\) for \(Aa\), and \(0.36\) for \(aa\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_2019_Q119 - Calculation of Respiratory Quotient value of tripalmitin

questiontext.text: Respiratory Quotient (RQ) value of tripalmitin is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Substance undergoing aerobic respiration: Tripalmitin (\(\text{C}_{51}\text{H}_{98}\text{O}_6\)), a triglyceride fat.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Respiratory Quotient (\(\text{RQ}\)) is the ratio of the volume of \(\text{CO}_2\) evolved to the volume of \(\text{O}_2\) consumed:
\[ \text{RQ} = \frac{\text{Volume of }\text{CO}_2\text{ evolved}}{\text{Volume of }\text{O}_2\text{ consumed}} \]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
1. Complete oxidation equation for tripalmitin:
\[ 2\text{C}_{51}\text{H}_{98}\text{O}_6 + 145\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 102\text{CO}_2 + 98\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Energy} \]
2. Substitute stoichiometric coefficients into the \(\text{RQ}\) formula:
\[ \text{RQ} = \frac{102\text{ CO}_2}{145\text{ O}_2} \approx 0.703 \]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Fats require more oxygen relative to carbon dioxide produced during respiration, resulting in an \(\text{RQ}\) value less than \(1.0\), specifically \(0.7\).

Steroid hormones (lipid-soluble) cross the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane and bind to intracellular receptors inside the nucleus. The hormone-receptor complex interacts with specific DNA sequences (genome) to regulate gene expression and protein synthesis.

Steroid hormones influence cellular activity by binding to DNA and forming a hormone-receptor/gene complex.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_2019_Q153 - Incorrect statement regarding annual rings in trees

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The assertion that annual rings are not prominent in trees of temperate regions is incorrect.

Phloem translocates organic solutes (sucrose/sugars) from source (site of synthesis/storage) to sink (site of utilization/storage).

Step 2: Source-Sink Dynamics
Because the source-sink relationship changes depending on plant developmental stage or season (e.g. from leaves to roots in summer, or from roots to growing buds in spring), movement of sugars in phloem is bi-directional.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The direction of sugar movement in phloem is bi-directional.

The shorter and longer arms are referred to as p-arm and q-arm respectively.

Burying the waste within rocks deep below the Earth's surface is the most suitable method.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_2019_Q175 - Calculation of heart rate from cardiac output and ventricular volumes

questiontext.text: What would be the heart rate of a person if the cardiac output is 5 L, blood volume in the ventricles at the end of diastole is 100 mL and at the end of ventricular systole is 50 ml ?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Cardiac Output (\(\text{CO}\)) = \(5\text{ L/min} = 5000\text{ mL/min}\)
- End-Diastolic Volume (\(\text{EDV}\)) = \(100\text{ mL}\)
- End-Systolic Volume (\(\text{ESV}\)) = \(50\text{ mL}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Stroke Volume (\(\text{SV}\)):
\[ \text{SV} = \text{EDV} - \text{ESV} \]
2. Cardiac Output (\(\text{CO}\)):
\[ \text{CO} = \text{Stroke Volume} \times \text{Heart Rate} \]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate Stroke Volume:
\[ \text{SV} = 100\text{ mL} - 50\text{ mL} = 50\text{ mL} \]
2. Calculate Heart Rate (\(\text{HR}\)):
\[ \text{HR} = \frac{\text{CO}}{\text{SV}} = \frac{5000\text{ mL/min}}{50\text{ mL}} = 100\text{ beats per minute} \]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
A stroke volume of \(50\text{ mL}\) multiplied by \(100\text{ beats/min}\) equals a cardiac output of \(5000\text{ mL/min}\) (\(5\text{ L/min}\)).
The heart rate is 100 beats per minute.
